title: ChatGPT, Esq.: Recasting Unauthorized Practice of Law in the Era of Generative AI
pub: Yale Journal of Law & Technology, vol. 26, no. 1, p. 64 (2024)
author: Joseph J. Avery · Patricia Sánchez Abril · Alissa del Riego

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source shares the cluster’s view that AI can expand access, but reframes the principal problem as UPL restrictions and monopoly pricing rather than downward risk transfer. It advances a substantially more optimistic case for autonomous AI substitution in some matters and does not substantively engage the cluster’s concerns about users’ limited verification capacity, weak remedies or unequal reliability.
qs: In sum, the most salient negative externality of UPL statutes is that they unfairly and overwhelmingly impact underprivileged individuals.

As even better LLMs are developed, and as ones geared especially for legal work are created, it is only a matter of time until the best, cheapest, and most efficient attorney for some matters will be an AI.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source acknowledges AI augmentation and task substitution, but shifts the central inquiry from bounded, verified workflow deployment and competence preservation to whether unauthorized-practice rules should permit AI-delivered legal services. Its stronger claims about independent legal advice and potential lawyer replacement do not accept the cluster’s supervised-copilot framing.
qs: And, lastly, LLMs can function in isolation, serving as full replacements for lawyers: think of Expedia and other software-as-a-service ("SaaS") companies that have diminished the need for traditional travel-agent professionals.
The Case for Dismantling UPL Rules  The case for dismantling UPL rules has never been stronger than it is today.

st.t: Provider reform: Competition cannot overcome every access barrier
st.an: The source foregrounds UPL restrictions as the principal access barrier and presents competition and AI-enabled services as likely consumer-welfare gains. Although it seeks clearer regulatory boundaries and consistent enforcement, it does not adopt the cluster’s broader emphasis on demand constraints, information asymmetry, ownership incentives, public duties, or outcome evidence.
qs: A Frustrated (or Perhaps False) Aim  If the stated aim of UPL rules is to benefit legal consumers, it is alarming that the bulk of the evidence suggests that UPL rules accomplish the exact opposite.
If bar associations want to stipulate UPL rules, at the very least they need to clearly define what is and is not a violation, and they need be consistent in identifying and litigating violations.

st.t: Regulatory sandboxes: Conditional entry tests consumer risk
st.an: The source shares the cluster’s access-to-justice objective but rejects conditional sandbox entry as the preferred mechanism. It instead proposes broad consumer freedom to use nonlawyer providers, relying on risk acknowledgement and tort liability rather than ex ante authorisation and risk-based oversight. Its claimed benefits are predictive rather than empirically demonstrated.
qs: Under our recommendation, consumers would be free to avail themselves of nonlawyer providers of legal services, acknowledging the risks inherent in relying upon an individual or entity who has not received bar certification.

In brief, legal technology companies would be freed from operating in a legal grey area; states would no longer have to create elaborate UPL-avoiding mechanisms, such as Utah's "sandbox"; consumers—both individuals and companies—would benefit from better and cheaper legal services; and solutions to long-standing access-to-justice problems would finally be within reach.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source rejects the cluster’s predominantly supervised-copilot framing for non-court legal services. It argues that AI can independently provide substantive legal advice and should be permitted to do so without lawyer oversight or status, while reserving representation in legal proceedings for licensed humans. This is a materially different regulatory model rather than a wholesale rejection of human accountability.
qs: In other words, this technology can, on its own, generate legal output, including the provision of legal advice.

However, any person or entity that wants to provide legal services—so long as they are not representing clients in legal proceedings—may do so to the extent they are not holding themselves out as lawyers.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source shifts the focus from selective, human-led deployment and workflow redesign to structural UPL reform. It treats AI not only as a copilot but as a potential standalone substitute and proposes broadly permitting AI and nonlawyers to deliver non-court legal services, with tort remedies and ethics rules addressing risks. This is a materially different regulatory framing rather than acceptance of the cluster’s cautious operating-model proposition.
qs: In permitting bar associations to remain the final arbiter of "lawyer" and "attorney" designations, and by allowing AI and other nonlawyers to provide any legal service besides representation in court proceedings, the stated aims of UPL rules will be best achieved.

And, lastly, LLMs can function in isolation, serving as full replacements for lawyers: think of Expedia and other software-as-a-service ("SaaS") companies that have diminished the need for traditional travel-agent professionals.

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central concern—expanding affordable legal assistance while preserving protection and accountability—and materially develops it through a specific title-based UPL regime: reserve lawyer designations and courtroom representation for licensed professionals while opening other legal services to AI and nonlawyers. It relies principally on informed consumer choice and tort liability, while acknowledging insurance, deception, inequality and implementation risks.
qs: In permitting bar associations to remain the final arbiter of "lawyer" and "attorney" designations, and by allowing AI and other nonlawyers to provide any legal service besides representation in court proceedings, the stated aims of UPL rules will be best achieved.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source directly supports the proposition that LLMs can complement lawyers through outsourced legal work and broader service delivery while also substituting for lawyers in some delivery models. Its examples are illustrative rather than systematic evidence of staffing, savings or aggregate employment effects.
qs: countries, lawyers now can cheaply and effortlessly outsource legal work to AI.

And, lastly, LLMs can function in isolation, serving as full replacements for lawyers: think of Expedia and other software-as-a-service ("SaaS") companies that have diminished the need for traditional travel-agent professionals.

kp.k: Generative AI performs core legal tasks
kp.d: The authors assert that GPT-4 can draft briefs and memoranda, develop litigation strategy, interpret statutes and provide tailored legal advice. They frame LLMs as potentially serving several roles: delivery medium, self-help research tool, outsourced legal worker, frequent lawyer collaborator or full lawyer substitute.
qs: GPT-4 has unprecedented ability to practice law: drafting briefs and memos, plotting litigation strategy, and providing general legal advice.

They can function as a means for licensed attorneys to outsource: just as Americans overwhelmingly outsourced tax preparation to individuals in non-U.S. countries, lawyers now can cheaply and effortlessly outsource legal work to AI.

And, lastly, LLMs can function in isolation, serving as full replacements for lawyers: think of Expedia and other software-as-a-service ("SaaS") companies that have diminished the need for traditional travel-agent professionals.

kp.k: Language models disrupt law’s traditional technological insulation
kp.d: The article argues that law was comparatively resistant to automation because its central medium is language rather than mathematics. LLMs remove that insulation by producing sophisticated text, enabling automation of work previously treated as intrinsically human legal reasoning and communication.
qs: Until recently, law was somewhat immune from the large technological disruptions felt in other domains, and this immunity was at least partly because law is not a mathematics-driven, computational field.
Rather, law "has language at its heart."
And language is a human endeavor, not an endeavor that is overly susceptible to technological encroachment—until the development of LLMs, that is.

kp.k: Existing UPL rules broadly restrict legal-service provision
kp.d: The authors describe UPL as generally prohibiting unlicensed people from representing others, preparing documents affecting legal rights or giving legal advice, while also restricting cross-jurisdictional practice and lawyers’ assistance to nonlawyers. Violations may attract injunctions, contempt findings and criminal penalties, although the precise state rules vary.
qs: As a general rule in all U.S. states, unless a person is a licensed attorney who has been admitted to the state bar after having met requirements of education, examination, and moral character, she may not represent another person in a legal matter.

"Practicing law" is not well-defined, although we argue that it certainly would include representation in legal proceedings, and it extends to preparing legal instruments or documents that affect the legal rights of others, as well as giving legal advice.
If one runs afoul of UPL rules, punishment may include injunctions, findings of contempt, quo warranto writs, and criminal penalties.

kp.k: UPL’s scope remains vague and inconsistently defined
kp.d: The article contends that neither courts nor the ABA have developed a workable definition of legal practice. This vagueness leaves providers uncertain about permissible conduct and, in the authors’ view, gives bar associations substantial discretion to pursue selected providers while tolerating comparable conduct elsewhere.
qs: A central tension can be gleaned from this discussion: there is an inappropriate vagueness that besets UPL enforcement.
That which qualifies as the practice of law has never been clearly delineated.
And so we are left with "broad and vague definitions of what does, and does not, constitute the practice of law."

kp.k: Longstanding exceptions weaken UPL’s stated rationale
kp.d: The authors identify tolerated legal work by paralegals, law librarians, law students, clerks, unadmitted associates, corporate officers and nonlawyer administrative representatives. They use these exceptions, especially Sperry, to argue that nonlawyers can sometimes match lawyers in competence and ethical conduct, undermining categorical restrictions.
qs: The Restatement makes these exceptions clear: "a nonlawyer undoubtedly may engage in some limited forms of law practice."

The Court approvingly cited a report stating that, in the patent office context, "[T]here is no significant difference between lawyers and nonlawyers, either with respect to their ability to handle the work or with respect to their ethical conduct."
The Sperry decision affirmed what was already clear: in some circumstances, nonlawyers may provide legal services without violating prohibitions of the unauthorized practice of law.

kp.k: UPL enforcement has constrained legal-technology providers
kp.d: The article traces UPL action against self-help books, document software, LegalZoom, Rasa Legal and DoNotPay. These examples are presented as evidence that legal technology providers operate in a regulatory gray area or require special mechanisms such as Utah’s 2020 legal-services sandbox.
qs: A Texas district court enjoined sale of the software program, holding that its services constituted the practice of law and were thus unauthorized.
For providing these services, LegalZoom was either sued or faced bar proceedings in multiple states, actions that hobbled the company and threatened its continued existence.

The only reason Rasa Legal is permitted to operate is because the state of Utah instituted a "legal services sandbox" in 2020—in essence, a free-pass from UPL claims for companies experimenting with using technology to overcome barriers to justice.

kp.k: Human-AI collaboration spans assistance through automation
kp.d: Using a cited taxonomy, the article classifies human-AI work as assisting, arresting, augmenting or automating, ordered by increasing agentic freedom. It maps spreadsheets and e-discovery to assistance, interactive document systems and smart contracts to action selection, advanced legal search to augmentation, and autonomous prediction or LLM-generated legal output to automation.
qs: AI may be "assisting," "arresting," "augmenting," or "automating."
These are ordered in terms of AI agentic freedom, going from least to most agentic.
The fourth type in the taxonomy is "automating" agentic collaboration, where the AI exercises intentionality over protocol development and action selection.

kp.k: AI complicates lawyer supervision and attribution
kp.d: The authors argue that AI increasingly performs work constituting legal practice while its contribution cannot readily be separated from the lawyer’s. They also report concerns that many lawyers lack the analytical capacity to verify whether tools such as e-discovery systems are suitable and operating correctly.
qs: This is in spite of the fact that most, if not all, lawyers do not possess the proper analytical tools "to assess whether a particular technology is adequate for the task and whether it is working properly when employed," raising questions about the scope of lawyer supervision.

It should now be evident—but it will become more evident still—that AI is rapidly subsuming tasks that constitute the practice of law, and disentangling humans from AI contributions is nearly impossible.
That is, most every law firm, most every individual attorney's practice, is or will be reliant upon AI that are violating UPL rules and cannot be reasonably overseen.

kp.k: One study projected seventy-percent lawyer-task exposure
kp.d: The article reports another study’s forward-looking exposure estimate, defining exposure as reducing task-completion time by at least 50%. That study projected that GPT-powered software could affect as much as 70% of lawyers’ tasks; the article does not present this as observed displacement or job loss.
qs: The authors looked at "exposure percentages," where exposure was defined as reducing the time it takes to complete a task by at least 50%.
They projected that as much as 70% of lawyers' tasks are exposed to GPT-powered software.

kp.k: Authors’ experiments found increasingly capable legal advice
kp.d: The authors report anecdotal tests conducted in early and mid-March 2023. An earlier ChatGPT version initially refused to draft a trespass brief but answered a reframed request; a GPT-4-based version later supplied tailored advice after a disclaimer. They characterize its interpretation, analysis and factual accuracy positively, but offer no systematic benchmark.
qs: In early March 2023, we asked ChatGPT to write a brief on the law of trespassing in Miami-Dade County, Florida.
Two weeks later, in mid-March 2023, we had access to an updated version of ChatGPT, one that is built atop GPT-4.
First, it displayed a solid grasp of statutory interpretation. Second, the legal analysis was thorough and methodical. Third, the advice showed factual accuracy.

kp.k: Technology adoption makes broad UPL enforcement impracticable
kp.d: The authors cite growth in listed legal startups from 15 in 2009 to more than 720 by January 2015, alongside consumer surveys indicating sustained demand for cheaper nonlawyer and online services. They infer that LLM-related UPL infractions are now widespread and that broad rules invite inequitable or selective enforcement.
qs: In 2009, only 15 legal startups were listed on the startup-related website, AngelList. By January 2015, the number had grown to more than 720 startups.
In a 1974 ABA survey, 82% of respondents agreed that "many things that lawyers handle—for example, tax matters or estate planning—can be done as well and less expensively by nonlawyers."
A study of over 2,000 adults aged 18-54 found that 76% of respondents "were willing to use online legal services for legal issues if it would save them money."

kp.k: UPL may protect incumbent lawyers’ economic interests
kp.d: The article presents economic protectionism as a plausible but difficult-to-prove explanation for broad UPL rules. It links restrictions to law firms’ hourly-billing incentives and reports arguments that bar regulation may delay machine intelligence, while acknowledging that attributing motives across institutions and decades is nearly impossible.
qs: Could UPL be substantially motivated by a desire to restrain the trade for the economic benefit of lawyers?
As Professors McGinnis and Pearce put it: "[t]he surest way for lawyers to retain the market power of old is to use bar regulation to delay and obstruct the use of machine intelligence."
But the question of economic protectionism is nearly impossible to answer, requiring one to intuit the motivations of countless parties across many years.

kp.k: UPL restrictions intensify the justice gap
kp.d: The authors argue that monopoly pricing and restrictions on nonlawyer services disproportionately deny low-income people legal help. Supporting figures include an ABA president’s 2015 estimate that 80% of the population lacked adequate access and a Legal Services Corporation estimate that costs prevented guidance for more than half of 1.7 million low-income legal issues in 2013.
qs: In 2015, ABA President William Hubbard estimated that 80% of the U.S. population lacked adequate access to legal services.

In 2013, the Legal Services Corporation estimated that low-income Americans had 1.7 million legal issues, and, for more than half of these issues, the cost of legal services would prohibit them from receiving requisite legal guidance.
In sum, the most salient negative externality of UPL statutes is that they unfairly and overwhelmingly impact underprivileged individuals.

kp.k: Automation can commoditize selected legal services
kp.d: The article describes a progression from bespoke work through standardization and systematization to packaged commodities. It predicts that, for tasks amenable to commoditization, specialized LLMs may eventually outperform lawyers on quality, price and efficiency by reducing noise and bias; this is expressly a prospective and conditional claim.
qs: Next, that which is standardized becomes systematized.
At some point, this standardized and systematized technology is packaged so that it can be bought and used by others. It becomes a commodity.

As even better LLMs are developed, and as ones geared especially for legal work are created, it is only a matter of time until the best, cheapest, and most efficient attorney for some matters will be an AI.

kp.k: Constitutional and antitrust pressures threaten current UPL
kp.d: The authors report due-process, occupational-freedom and First Amendment arguments against licensing restrictions, particularly because legal services consist largely of speech. They also invoke Goldfarb and North Carolina State Board of Dental Examiners to argue that professional regulators controlled by market participants may face antitrust constraints.
qs: Since the dawn of the so-called Information Age, vocations have become increasingly expressive. This is even more true for legal services, where the work product is nothing but speech.
Importantly, courts do not apply the rational-basis test when free speech is implicated. Rather, they apply some form of heightened scrutiny.
"Active market participants" who regulate their own markets now are on notice that they face liability for antitrust violations.

kp.k: Protect lawyer titles instead of most legal tasks
kp.d: The article’s principal recommendation is to recast UPL as regulation of entity-type claims. Bar associations would continue determining who may use “lawyer” or “attorney” designations, while people, companies and AI systems could provide other legal services if they do not represent themselves as licensed lawyers.
qs: First, rather than controlling provision of legal services, bar associations should primarily control lawyer designations (that is, which individuals can call themselves lawyers).
At the same time, nonlawyers would be free to provide legal services, which have never been sufficiently delineated anyhow.
However, nonlawyers would not be allowed to explicitly or implicitly hold themselves out as "lawyers" or "attorneys."

kp.k: Court representation should remain lawyer-exclusive
kp.d: The proposed exception would reserve representation in legal proceedings to licensed lawyers. The authors justify this boundary through historical precedent, courtroom interpersonal demands and the heightened moral significance of proceedings affecting liberty or life, while predicting that AI will not soon replicate human connection and persuasion effectively.
qs: UPL rules should continue to forbid nonlawyers from providing some legal services.
Here, we are referring to a clearly defined subset of legal services—representation in legal proceedings.
Only lawyers will be able to provide legal representation.

kp.k: Rules 5.3 and 5.5 require targeted revision
kp.d: The authors recommend changing Rule 5.3’s references from a nonlawyer “person” to a “person or entity,” expressly covering AI and legal-technology companies. Rule 5.5 should separate jurisdiction-specific lawyer status from the broader provision of legal services, allowing nonlawyer entities to serve consumers outside legal proceedings.
qs: Rule 5.3 repeatedly refers to the nonlawyer as a "person," which should be changed to "person or entity" to include AI and legal technology companies that might be serving as the nonlawyer.

However, any person or entity that wants to provide legal services—so long as they are not representing clients in legal proceedings—may do so to the extent they are not holding themselves out as lawyers.
Said again, providing legal services does not redesignate providers as lawyers.

kp.k: Tort liability would discipline nonlawyer legal providers
kp.d: Rather than relying principally on occupational gatekeeping, the authors recommend negligence, deceptive-practices and false-advertising liability for deficient alternative legal services. They predict that private rights of action would create stronger competency incentives and force courts to articulate service-specific standards of care.
qs: As others have argued, the tort system is fully equipped to achieve this end in the absence of UPL rules.
As per our recommendation, consumers of legal services would have a private right of action against any party that provides legal services.
A move towards the torts system would ensure greater focus on what matters: the quality of the legal services provided to consumers.

kp.k: Technology may require federalized provider ethics
kp.d: The article argues that cross-border technology-driven services may require a common ethics code covering lawyers and nonlawyers, rather than inconsistent state-only rules. It separately reports that e-discovery, prediction and advanced analytics are already prompting adaptation of specific civil-procedure rules.
qs: Regardless of the future of UPL, legal technology is necessitating significant changes in civil procedure.
In addition, there may be a need for at least some code of legal ethics that applies to providers of legal services—lawyers and nonlawyers alike.

A federal code of ethics for legal providers, as opposed to state-level codes, would create the consistency needed when legal service providers are technology-driven, since their tools will operate across state lines.

kp.k: Reform carries unresolved distributional and market risks
kp.d: The authors acknowledge uncertainty about insurance coverage, fraudulent notario-style schemes, declining legal fees, talent leaving law and unequal uptake favoring educated or affluent users. These are presented as open questions and possible unintended consequences, not established outcomes.
qs: There will be many more considerations that emerge: nonlawyers who provide legal services will be less likely to carry malpractice insurance; with nonlawyers permitted to provide legal services, will there be an increase in notario-style ploys?; will there be such a precipitous drop in legal fees that talented individuals leave the legal field altogether?; and although our recommendation appears poised to resolve many access-to-justice issues, is it possible that our policy will disproportionately benefit individuals who are either well-educated or well-off?

Such recasting comes with the prospect of unintended consequences, and unintended legal consequences are daunting because they may touch upon such essentialities as livelihood, liberty, family—everything that law involves.

kp.k: AI pressures information-monopoly practices, not all law
kp.d: The conclusion frames generative AI as a catalyst for regulatory reform and wider access rather than a threat to every form of legal practice. The authors contend that its primary target is expensive practice built around exclusive control of legal information, while predicting that permitting alternative providers will help address unmet legal needs.
qs: Indeed, autoregressive LLMs are transformative, but they threaten only the information-monopolizing type of legal practice that is failing consumers.
AI may be a useful invention that hastens much-needed legal reform and improves access to legal services.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Avery, Sánchez Abril, and del Riego claim that LLMs already perform substantive legal work and can support lawyers, enable self-help, or replace lawyers for some purposes.
pts.d: The authors describe GPT-4 drafting briefs and memoranda, developing litigation strategy, and giving tailored advice. They distinguish several uses: facilitating professional advice, supporting clients' own research, allowing lawyers to outsource work to AI, and operating independently as lawyer substitutes. Their independent-use scenario includes a person obtaining AI advice and then representing herself pro se; it is distinct from AI formally representing someone in court. They describe increasingly capable models as becoming frequent and nearly essential collaborators.

pts.k: The authors anticipate extensive task automation and argue that productivity gains create tension with hourly billing.
pts.d: They cite an external projection that up to 70% of lawyers' tasks are exposed to GPT-powered software, where exposure means a potential reduction in task completion time of at least 50%, not elimination of that share of jobs. They argue that existing automation, including document generation, should produce time savings and lower client fees, but identify a conflict between clients' cost-control goals and firms' hourly billing incentives. They do not provide a quantified forecast of employment losses or fee reductions.

pts.k: The authors predict that AI can outperform lawyers in some commoditized services, reducing cost, inconsistency, and potentially bias.
pts.d: Their argument follows a progression from bespoke work to standardization, systematization, and commoditization. They claim that commoditized services may be higher quality because performance varies less, and predict that improving and legally specialized LLMs will become the best and cheapest option for some matters. This is a task-specific claim, not a claim that AI is superior across all legal practice. Bias reduction is conditional on proper development and deployment.

pts.k: The authors argue that AI adoption makes existing UPL restrictions increasingly untenable and susceptible to selective enforcement.
pts.d: They claim AI is absorbing activities constituting legal practice, that separating human and machine contributions is becoming nearly impossible, and that many practices already rely or will rely on AI that cannot reasonably be overseen under existing rules. They characterize widespread UPL infractions as an assumption arising from widespread tool use and inadequate oversight, rather than reporting a measured incidence rate. In their account, UPL restrictions obstruct beneficial services without preventing adoption and give bar associations discretion to target providers.

pts.k: The authors predict that allowing AI and other nonlawyers to supply most legal services would improve access and competition while preserving lawyer titles and courtroom representation.
pts.d: Their proposed reform primarily regulates claims to be a lawyer or attorney, rather than reserving all legal services to licensed lawyers. Representation in legal proceedings would remain reserved. They predict better and cheaper services, less legal uncertainty for technology companies, less need for sandboxes, and weaker free-speech and antitrust challenges. They also argue that negligence liability would incentivize competence more effectively than entry credentials alone. These are projected consequences of their proposal, not reported outcomes of its implementation. Separately, they suggest technology requires procedural adaptation and may warrant a federal ethics code covering lawyer and nonlawyer providers.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Capability claims rest on reported exam performance, an external task-exposure projection, and the authors' own March 2023 prompting experience.
pts.d: The article reports GPT-4 scoring above 90% of human Uniform Bar Exam test takers. It also cites the external 70% task-exposure projection without presenting its underlying methods in the supplied text. The authors' hands-on evidence concerns Florida trespass prompts in early and mid-March 2023: they report an initial refusal overcome by rephrasing and a later GPT-4 response offering specific advice after a disclaimer. They assess that response as accurate, methodical, and strong on statutory interpretation. These examples are not presented as a systematic evaluation of real-world legal outcomes, and the article provides no quantified comparative test supporting its broader superiority and bias-reduction claims.

pts.k: The regulatory and access claims draw on litigation, reported enforcement threats, surveys, access estimates, and legal-economic reasoning rather than a direct test of the proposed reform.
pts.d: The authors use DoNotPay's abandoned 2023 courtroom-assistance plan, historical actions against Quicken and LegalZoom, and Rasa Legal's operation in Utah's sandbox to illustrate regulatory barriers. Quicken and LegalZoom are precedents concerning legal software, not evidence of GPT-4 performance. They invoke Sperry and antitrust cases in constructing their reform argument. For demand and unmet need, they cite a 1974 ABA survey, a later survey of over 2,000 adults aged 18–54, a 2015 estimate from ABA President William Hubbard, and 2013 Legal Services Corporation estimates. These establish the authors' contextual basis for expecting benefits; they do not measure AI's actual reduction of the justice gap. Their predictions about reform, tort incentives, prices, and constitutional challenges are principally legal and policy arguments.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article combines March 2023 observations with undated forecasts conditioned on model improvement, regulatory reform, and limits on courtroom substitution.
pts.d: Published in 2024, the article treats substantive LLM assistance and automation as already available, while giving no deadline for AI to become the best option for particular matters. Its strongest access and competition predictions depend on adopting the proposed UPL changes. The authors retain a near-term boundary around courtroom representation because of interpersonal demands and morally significant stakes. They acknowledge unintended consequences and pose unresolved questions about insurance, fraud, departures from the profession if fees fall, and unequal distribution of benefits; these are possibilities, not forecasts that such outcomes will occur.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The authors identify low-income people as the principal access-to-justice beneficiaries, alongside broader effects on clients, lawyers, providers, and regulators.
pts.d: Individuals unable to afford lawyers could obtain advice and support for self-representation, including housing, traffic, and expungement matters. Businesses could also obtain cheaper services, a benefit distinct from closing unmet individual legal need. Lawyers and firms would gain drafting, research, and automation support while facing competition in commoditized work and tension with hourly billing. Legal technology companies and nonlawyer service providers would gain clearer permission to operate, coupled with potential tort liability. Bar associations would retain control of professional designations but lose their broader service monopoly under the proposal; states would have less need for special regulatory workarounds. The authors do not quantify effects by firm size, seniority, or employment category.
